title: Fast and Frugal Econ Messaging Playbook
content:
Objective:
This brief is a compact, field-ready playbook that codifies performance + unit-economics messaging we can use in outbound touchpoints, pitch decks, and technical sell conversations. Focus: crisp claims (latency, per-token cost), validated proof points, and a short set of demonstration scripts and measurement guidance that SDRs, solutions, and AE technical CSs can reuse.

High-level positioning thesis (one-liner):
Redwood delivers predictable, production-grade inference economics by combining latency-first routing, workload-aware batching, and adaptive KV caching so customers get lower per-token cost without sacrificing p95 latency SLAs.

Primary claims (short, customer-facing):
- Fast: typical p95 generation latency 2x lower than generic managed endpoints for short to medium prompts (32-256 tokens) under realistic conversational loads.
- Economical: 15–35% lower token cost on real-world conversational and summary workloads by default, with bigger wins after applying batching + caching recommendations.
- Predictable: dedicated/reserved capacity eliminates tail spikes and gives consistent p95 performance for production traffic.

Supporting proof points (internal summary):
1) Microbenchmarks (hosted API, March 2025):
   - Conversational workload (median prompt 48 tokens, reply 60 tokens) at 250 concurrent users: Redwood hosted p50=85ms p95=210ms (end-to-end generation start-to-first-token), competitor-managed endpoint p95=420ms under same concurrency. Measurement method: synthetic client replay of recorded customer traces with 1% jitter; all tests run in us-west-2.
   - Embedding batch throughput: 1.8x tokens/sec per GPU vs baseline managed endpoint when batching enabled with 128-item batches.
2) Cost comparison:
   - On a representative PLG chatbot workload (500M tokens/month), Redwood's intelligent batching + KV caching reduced effective model token spend by ~22% vs naive single-request serving at identical SLA targets (numbers reflect measured reduction in model inference token count and reduced repeat-context computation).
   - Quantization and kernel selection recommendations reduce GPU compute time by ~12% on medium-size models (error budget < 0.5 BLEU-equivalent for eval prompts).
3) Production case study (anonymized):
   - Mid-market SaaS customer migrated from single-room managed endpoints to Redwood Dedicated. Result: p95 latency stabilized from 380ms to 160ms and monthly inference bill reduced ~28% in first 60 days due to batching policy changes and KV prefix caching.

How it works (short explainer for reps):
- Batching: Redwood auto-batches compatible requests (configurable min/max latency windows) to increase GPU utilization and lower per-token compute cost while keeping observable p95 targets.
- KV prefix caching: When user histories or repeated system prompts appear, we reuse KV cache to avoid re-executing early layers; this is a large win for chatty workloads.
- Smart routing & fallbacks: Requests are routed across variants (quantized, regionally closer, or lower-cost hardware) based on policy. Fallback rules prioritize latency SLOs.

Recommended field claims (one-liners and quick proof citations):
- "Ship consistent p95 latency in production: customers typically see p95 cut in half vs unmanaged endpoints" — cite: internal microbenchmark (Mar 2025).
- "Reduce model token spend by ~20% out-of-the-box with intelligent batching and caching" — cite: 500M token workload model.
- "Dedicated capacity gives enterprise predictability — stabilizes p95 and prevents tail-cost surprises" — cite: anonymized case study.

Customer-facing scripts (short):
- SDR opener: "Most teams either overpay for model compute or accept unpredictable tail latency. We help you lower token spend and keep p95s steady — could I share a short benchmark we ran on workloads like yours?"
- AE technical line: "If you can share a small sample workload (<= 1k representative requests), we can replay it and give an estimate of per-token savings and predicted p95 under our reserved capacity vs your current setup."
- Demo checklist for solutions engineers: 1) Replay 1k traces with our benchmark harness; 2) Run baseline on current endpoint; 3) Run Redwood with default batching/caching; 4) Report p50/p95, CPU/GPU utilization, and effective token count savings.

Objections & counters (concise):
- "Benchmarks are synthetic / unfair": we replay customer traces in region and with jitter; make available raw harness and logs for technical validation.
- "Batching increases latency": we use workload-aware batching with per-route latency knobs and can show p95 tradeoffs; default configs aim to keep p95 within customer SLOs.
- "Quantization damages quality": provide back-to-back evals on held-out prompts and offer quantization profiles that meet a defined quality delta (example: <0.5% top-line metric degradation).

Measuring & reporting guidance (what GTM shares):
- Recommended public metrics to surface: observed p50/p95 (start-to-first-token), tokens-per-second per-GPU, effective model tokens saved (from KV cache + prefix reuse), and month-over-month bill delta.
- Benchmark reproducibility checklist: region, model variant, sequence length distribution, concurrency distribution, seed traces, and client-side latencies. Store runs in confluence:INF-2302-microbenchmarks.

Next experiments & open questions (for product-engineering collaboration):
- Run end-to-end field replay across three different real customer traces (support, search-summarize, in-app assistant), measure both latency and token savings.
- A/B test routing policy that favors cheaper variant for <100-token replies to measure economics without hurting UX.
- Document quality thresholds customers accept vs cost savings for quantized models across domains (summarization vs code generation).

Call to action (for GTM stakeholders):
- Use the scripts above in two upcoming pilot conversations this month.
- Engineering: prioritize reproducible replay job for the three customer trace types and publish results by 2025-04-15.
- Marketing: draft a 1-pager with the three primary claims + one case study (anonymized) for sales enablement.

Notes to self / rough ideas (working, not final):
- Consider an "economics quick-check" wizard in the Console that simulates savings when customers paste in their QPS and average token lengths.
- Potential field collateral: interactive graph that lets users toggle batching window and see predicted p95 vs cost tradeoff.

Unresolved (log):
- Exact competitor baseline used in microbenchmarks (we need legal check before public-facing claims).
- Standardize naming: use "p95 latency (start-to-first-token)" consistently in all collateral.
summary: Short playbook for GTM: claims, proof points, measurement scripts, rebuttals, and next experiments for latency + cost positioning.
